---
name: fact-check
description: Check whether a claim, rumour, forwarded message, news item, statistic, quote or "did you know" is true - saying what is established, what is doubtful, what is false, how sure you are and why, and how the user can verify it themselves.
---
# Checking a claim

Use this when the user asks "is it true that", "is this real", "fact check", pastes a forwarded message or a screenshot and asks whether to believe it, or asks whether a number or quote is right.

Steps:
1. Restate the claim in one sentence, exactly as it stands, and split it if it is really two claims.
2. Give the verdict in the first line with one of five words: true, mostly true, unclear, misleading, false. Then your confidence: high, medium, low.
3. Explain in 3 to 6 lines what is known: the established fact, the part that is right, the part that is wrong or twisted, the missing context. Keep known facts and your reasoning apart ("it is known that ... / from that I conclude ...").
4. Say how sure you are and why: you know it well; it is widely documented; it changes often (prices, laws, officials, records); it is after what you know; you cannot see the picture or the source.
5. Give 2 or 3 ways to verify: the kind of source that settles it (the official statistics office, the manufacturer's page, the original study, the law's text, a reverse image search), not a vague "check reputable sources".
6. For a forwarded message or a chain message: list the usual signs (urgency, "share with everyone", no date, no named source, a too-good or too-scary number) that are present.

Defaults:
- Never state as fact what you are not sure of. A guess is marked as a guess. If you do not know, say "I don't know" and give the way to check.
- Dates: things after your knowledge may have changed; say so when the claim is about recent events, prices, laws or people in office.
- Quotes: a quote is "attributed" unless you know the source; famous people get misquoted; say that.
- Statistics: ask what the number is a share of, over what time, from which source; a true number can be misleading without that.
- Health, money, safety claims: add the one practical consequence (do not stop a medicine on a forwarded message; call the bank on the number on your card, not the one in the message).

Output template:
Claim: <one sentence>
Verdict: <word>, confidence <high/medium/low>.
What is known: ...
Why this confidence: ...
Check it yourself: 1 ... 2 ... 3 ...

Example:
User: "Is it true we only use 10 % of our brain?"
Good answer: "Claim: humans use only 10 % of the brain. Verdict: false, confidence high. What is known: brain scans show activity in nearly all areas over a day; damage to almost any region causes some loss; the brain uses about 20 % of the body's energy, which it would not for unused tissue. The myth is old and often linked to self-help advertising. Check it yourself: a neuroscience textbook's chapter on brain imaging; the website of a national brain research institute; search 'ten percent myth' with 'neuroscience'."

Do:
- Give the verdict first; readers stop after the first line.
- Separate the true part of a mixed claim from the false part.
Don't:
- Don't invent sources, studies, numbers or URLs.
- Don't say "experts agree" without saying who.
- Don't lecture about misinformation; just check the claim.

Before you answer, check: verdict word and confidence in line one; known and concluded kept apart; the reason for the confidence; concrete ways to verify; no invented source.
